# TypeScript - Prerequisites check

**No new TypeScript today** - the API mechanics are all Playwright. Two things you have met get
used hard enough to be worth naming.

| In play | Taught in |
|---|---|
| `async` / `await`, Promises | [week3/day3_1](/learn/w3/d3/p1) |
| Nested property access | [day2_1](/learn/w7/d2/p1) |
| Template literals | [week6/day3_1](/learn/w6/d3/p1) |
| `any` from `JSON.parse` | [week5/day5_1](/learn/w5/d5/p1) |
| Typed callback parameters | below |

**Next:** [Fundamentals - Your first API tests](/learn/w7/d3/p2)

## Typing a callback parameter

`JSON.parse` gives you `any`, so `.map()` over it has no idea what an item is. Annotating the
parameter is how you get checking back for one line.

```ts
const isbns = body.books.map((b: { isbn: string }) => b.isbn);
```

`{ isbn: string }` is an **inline type**: this parameter is an object with an `isbn` that is a
string. Nothing else about the item is claimed.

## Two awaits, not one

This is the shape that confuses everyone on their first API test. **Each step is its own
Promise.**

| Line | What is awaited |
|---|---|
| `const response = await request.get(url)` | the round trip to the server |
| `const body = await response.json()` | reading and parsing the body |

Forget the second `await` and you get a `Promise` object where you expected data - and the
assertion fails with something that looks nothing like the cause.

# Fundamentals - Your first API tests

By the end of this lesson you will have read a collection, read one item, checked a negative
case, created a user and fetched a token - with **no browser launched at all**.

> **Follow this one in your own project.** These examples are run by the Playwright test runner, which the editor here does not provide. Copy them into your own checkout to run them.

## `request` instead of `page`

That is the entire structural difference from every test you have written.

| UI test | API test |
|---|---|
| `async ({ page }) => {` | `async ({ request }) => {` |
| `page` drives a browser | `request` sends HTTP |
| `await page.goto(url)` | `await request.get(url)` |
| assert on visible things | assert on status and body |

Everything else - `test`, `expect`, `describe`, hooks, config - is unchanged. And it is built in:
Selenium needs a separate library for this, Playwright does not.

## Where the file goes

```
week7/generated/
  day3-first-api.spec.ts
```

A `testDir` or `testMatch` in a config can point at an API-only folder, exactly as in
[week5/day1_2](/learn/w5/d1/p2) - handy when you want the fast suite to be *only* the API
tests.

## What each step showed

| Step | Point |
|---|---|
| 1 | `response.status()` is verification one of two |
| 2 | two ways to read a body - one is shorter |
| 3 | `books` is the parent; you cannot skip to `isbn` |
| 4 | one resource, and asserting the **body** as well as the code |
| 5 | the negative case answers **400**, not 404 |
| 6 | `POST` carries `data`, and answers **201** |
| 7 | a token you cannot predict, so `toBeTruthy()` |

## Step 2, in detail: `.text()` versus `.json()`

```ts
const viaText = JSON.parse(await response.text());   // the session's version
const viaJson = await response.json();               // shorter, and typed better
```

| | `JSON.parse(await response.text())` | `await response.json()` |
|---|---|---|
| Lines | two operations | one |
| On a non-JSON body | throws `Unexpected token` | throws too |
| On an **empty** body | throws | throws - see [day4_2](/learn/w7/d4/p2) Step 6 |
| Use it when | you want the raw text as well | almost always |

Prefer `.json()`. Reach for `.text()` when you need to look at what actually arrived - which is
exactly what you do when a body is not JSON.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 6, in detail: `data` is the body

```ts
await request.post(`${BASE_URL}/Account/v1/User`, {
  data: { userName, password },
});
```

`data` takes an object and Playwright serialises it to JSON **and** sets `Content-Type:
application/json` for you. Written by hand that is two more lines and a common mistake.

| Verb | Sends `data`? |
|---|---|
| `get` | no |
| `post` / `put` / `patch` | **yes** |
| `delete` | usually not - though this API is an exception, see [day4_2](/learn/w7/d4/p2) |

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## The serial-mode trap in that spec

The POST block carries one extra line:

```ts
test.describe.configure({ mode: "serial" });
```

Without it, the repo's `fullyParallel: true` puts Steps 6 and 7 in **different workers**. Each
computes its own `userName`, so Step 7 asks for a token for a user that was never created and
fails with `token: null` - which looks like an API bug and is not one.

That failure was real while this lesson was being written. Serial mode came from
[week3/day2_2](/learn/w3/d2/p2); `beforeAll` is the better answer, and it is
[day4_2](/learn/w7/d4/p2).

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom |
|---|---|
| Forgetting the second `await` | assertions run against a `Promise` |
| Asserting only the status | see [day2_2](/learn/w7/d2/p2) Step 6 |
| Sharing state between parallel tests | `null` where you expected a value |
| A fixed username on a shared sandbox | passes once, then 406 forever |
| Not cleaning up what you created | you are a guest on a public API |

**Next:** [Implementation - The same calls, tidied up](/learn/w7/d3/p3)

# Implementation - The same calls, tidied up

Same `request.get`, same `expect` - arranged so a suite of two hundred API tests stays readable.

## Three things repeat in every API spec

| Repeated | Fix |
|---|---|
| `https://demoqa.com` in every URL | a `baseURL`, set once |
| `Authorization: Bearer ...` | one helper - [day5_2](/learn/w7/d5/p2) |
| create-a-user-then-get-a-token | `beforeAll` - [day4_2](/learn/w7/d4/p2) |

The first one Playwright already handles.

## `baseURL` works for API tests too

```ts
// playwright.config.ts, or a config of its own
use: { baseURL: "https://demoqa.com" }
```

Then a test says only the endpoint:

```ts
await request.get("/BookStore/v1/Books");
```

| | Full URL in each test | `baseURL` in config |
|---|---|---|
| Moving to a staging host | edit every test | edit one line |
| Reading the test | noisy | the endpoint stands out |

This week's specs spell out `BASE_URL` as a constant instead, so each file is self-contained and
runnable on its own - a teaching choice, not the one to copy into a real suite.

That is the same `process.env` idea as [week3/day5_3](/learn/w3/d5/p3), now deciding a host
rather than a browser.

## Give the response a type

`await response.json()` returns `any`. Describing the shape once turns every later typo into a
compile error.

```ts
type Book = { isbn: string; title: string; author: string };
type BooksResponse = { books: Book[] };

const body = (await response.json()) as BooksResponse;
body.books[0].titel;    // tsc: Property 'titel' does not exist on type 'Book'
```

| | `any` | a named type |
|---|---|---|
| Typo in a field | `undefined` at run time | **compile error** |
| Editor autocomplete | nothing | the real fields |
| Cost | none | four lines, once |

`as` only *claims* the shape - it checks nothing at run time
([week5/day5_1](/learn/w5/d5/p1)). It still catches the typos, which is most of the value.

# Practice - Practice

Write specs into `week7/generated/`. If you create anything on the API, **delete it afterwards** -
it is a shared public sandbox.
**Next:** [Day 4 - TypeScript - Prerequisites](/learn/w7/d4/p1)

problems.statement:
**Every book has the fields it should**
Write a test that fetches all books and asserts every one has a non-empty `isbn`, `title` and
`author`.

**Right when:** it passes, and you can say how many books were checked without hard-coding the
number.

**Forget an await**
Deliberately drop the `await` before `response.json()` and run it.

**Right when:** you can quote the failure and explain why it names the assertion rather than the
missing keyword.

**Type the response**
Add `type Book` and `type BooksResponse` per [day3_3](/learn/w7/d3/p3), then introduce a typo in a
field name.

**Right when:** `npx tsc --noEmit` catches it - and you can say why the lesson kernel would not.

**Three negative lookups**
Call the single-book endpoint with: an unknown ISBN, a blank ISBN, and no ISBN parameter at all.

**Right when:** you have three statuses, and at least one of them surprised you.

**A POST that should fail**
Create a user with a password that breaks the rules. Read the message carefully.

**Right when:** you assert the status **and** the message, and can list every rule the password
must satisfy.

**Prove there is no browser**
Run your API spec with `--headed`.

**Right when:** nothing opens, and you can explain why the flag is simply ignored.

**Time the difference**
Write one API test and one UI test that check the same fact, then compare the durations.

**Right when:** you have both numbers and a ratio - and you can say what the UI test checks that
the API one cannot.
